standard_prerequisites.name: Mere proposition
standard_prerequisites.statement: \isprop(A) is the type \prd{x,y:A} (x=y), so a proof of it is a function assigning a path to every pair.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the type whose propositionality is proved.

standard_prerequisites.name: Set
standard_prerequisites.statement: \isset(A) is the type \prd{x,y:A} \isprop(x=y), i.e. every path type of A is a mere proposition.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the second type whose propositionality is proved.

standard_prerequisites.name: Function extensionality and the set level
standard_prerequisites.statement: Two functions are equal as soon as they are equal pointwise, and a mere proposition is a set so its path types are mere propositions.
standard_prerequisites.use: They reduce both proofs to a pointwise comparison of paths (source lines 337-345).

core_obligations: For f, g : \isprop(A), use function extensionality to reduce f = g to f(x,y) = g(x,y) for all x, y : A (source lines 337-339).

Conclude that comparison because both f(x,y) and g(x,y) are paths in A, and A is a mere proposition by either f or g, hence a set by thm:prop-set, so its path types are mere propositions (source lines 339-342).

Repeat the argument for f, g : \isset(A): the pointwise comparison is now between proofs f(a,b,p,q) and g(a,b,p,q) of p = q, which are equal because A is a set by either f or g and hence a 1-type, and conclude again by function extensionality (source lines 342-345).

proof_roadmap.step: Reduce f = g to a pointwise comparison by function extensionality.
Settle the pointwise comparison for \isprop(A) through the set level of a mere proposition.
Repeat for \isset(A), where the comparison is between paths between paths.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 334-336 (book Theorem 3.3.5): for every type A the types \isprop(A) and \isset(A) are mere propositions. The statement gives no reason, and the proof (source lines 337-346) has to run the level bookkeeping twice. For \isprop(A) it reduces the equality of two proofs f and g by function extensionality to a comparison of the paths f(x,y) and g(x,y) in A, and those are equal only because either f or g makes A a mere proposition, which by thm:prop-set is then a set, so that paths in A are compared as elements of a mere proposition. For \isset(A) the comparison is one level higher: f and g are now functions sending a triple (a,b,p,q) to a path between paths, and the equality of their values uses that A is a set by either of them, hence a 1-type; function extensionality then closes the argument. The whole content is the interaction between the two level notions, which the statement does not mention.
